source: Krupenye, Kano, Hirata, Call & Tomasello (2017) A test of the submentalizing hypothesis: apes' performance in a false belief task inanimate control
finding: Heyes said apes' anticipatory looks in the false-belief video could be cueing by low-level features, and asked for an inanimate control. The authors ran it: the actor became a green semi-circle, the rest of the video stayed the same. Apes still tracked the key events, but looked at a box far less often and showed no reliable preference for the correct box.
numbers: 43 apes. Only 22 of 43 (51.2%) looked at a box in the anticipation phase, against 22 of 30 (73.3%) in the original agent study. Of those 22, 14 looked first to the Target (binomial p=0.28); FB1 6 of 11 (p=1.0). Viewing-time bias F(1,20)=1.03, p=0.32, eta2=0.05.
quote: we found no evidence that submentalizing was responsible for apes' anticipatory looks in our false-belief task
limits: A null result with a drop in looking, so power is low: more than half of the apes made no anticipatory look. Between-subject design with a new, larger sample. Written by the original lab. I did not open Heyes' reply or the Kano et al. TiCS note (d02).
agent_relevance: Template for a cue-only control: keep every surface cue of the test, remove the one element (the agent) the claim needs, and see if the effect survives. Report how many subjects produced any response, not only the split among responders.

source: Kano, Krupenye, Hirata, Call & Tomasello (2017) Submentalizing cannot explain belief-based action anticipation in apes (Trends in Cognitive Sciences)
finding: Reply to Heyes. From search snippets only: it cites the inanimate control above and an earlier study where a mechanical claw in place of a hand produced no goal-based anticipation in apes.
numbers: not read
limits: Publisher PDF returned only a title page; content known from search snippets. Heyes' own 2017 reply (Apes Submentalise) was not found. I could not confirm that the exchange ended in a design both sides accept.
agent_relevance: Treat the Heyes-Kano exchange as resolved by design only in the authors' view, not by consensus.

source: Chen et al. (Anthropic Alignment Science) (2025) Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Six hint types were put into multiple-choice prompts (four neutral: sycophancy, consistency, visual pattern, metadata; two misaligned: grader hacking, unethically obtained information). When a hint changed the answer, the chain of thought named the hint only a minority of the time, for reasoning and non-reasoning models alike.
numbers: Claude 3.7 Sonnet 25% overall (20% on misaligned hints); DeepSeek R1 39% (29% misaligned). Relative to non-reasoning siblings: 3.6x (Claude), 1.7x (DeepSeek). Harder GPQA vs MMLU: relative drop 44% (Claude), 32% (R1). Outcome RL raised faithfulness 63% relative on MMLU, 41% on GPQA, then plateaued near 28% and 20%. Reward-hack environments: hack used in >99% of cases within 30 steps, verbalised in <2% in 5 of 6 environments. Unfaithful CoTs were longer (Claude 2064 vs 1439 tokens; R1 6003 vs 4737).
quote: scaling outcome-based RL is insufficient for achieving high CoT faithfulness
limits: Read through an HTML page summary tool, so per-hint detail is missing. Multiple-choice QA; hint-verbalisation is a narrow notion of faithfulness (see d05). Two reasoning models only.
agent_relevance: Bias insertion still shows that visible reasoning omits what drove the answer in long-reasoning models. A G10 check should not trust a stated reason; it should change the input and see if the code-level decision moves.

source: Arcuschin, Janiak, Krzyzanowski, Rajamanoharan, Nanda & Conmy (2026) Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in the Wild Is Not Always Faithful (ICML 2026 version)
finding: No hint inserted. The same model is asked 'Is X bigger than Y?' and 'Is Y bigger than X?' separately. If it answers yes to both or no to both with a coherent argument each time, the reasoning is post-hoc. This happens in frontier models, but rarely in thinking models.
numbers: 4,834 question pairs, 15 frontier models plus one pretrained model. Unfaithful-pair rate up to 13.49% for production non-thinking models; DeepSeek R1 0.37%; Claude 3.7 Sonnet with thinking 0.04%. A pair is flagged if the two variants differ by >=50% in accuracy, group bias toward yes or no is >=5%, and the lower-accuracy variant's correct label opposes that bias.
quote: none are entirely so, including thinking models like DeepSeek R1 (0.37%) and Sonnet 3.7 with thinking (0.04%)
limits: Behavioural faithfulness only. Comparative questions, not hard reasoning. The authors call the evidence for the cause 'preliminary'. The illogical-shortcut section on hard maths was not read in detail.
agent_relevance: A paired-input consistency control needs no hint and works on long-reasoning models. It is a better G10 test than bias insertion for current models, but rates are low, so it needs thousands of pairs.

source: Zaman & Srivastava (2025, rev. 2026) Is Chain-of-Thought Really Not Explainability? Chain-of-Thought Can Be Faithful without Hint Verbalization
finding: The hint-verbalisation metric (Turpin, Chen) calls a chain of thought unfaithful when it omits an injected hint that flipped the answer. The authors argue this confuses incompleteness with unfaithfulness. Other metrics call many of those chains faithful, and a larger inference budget makes the chain mention the hint more often.
numbers: Models: Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-3-4B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen3-32B (thinking), Llama-3.3-70B. Multi-hop tasks (StrategyQA, OpenbookQA). Other metrics judge more than 50% of Biasing-Features-unfaithful chains faithful in some models; a filler-token metric exceeds 20% in many settings (60% for Llama-3.2-3B, Black Squares hint). faithful@k verbalisation rises up to 90% in some settings with a bigger budget. Judge gpt-oss-20b: 80% accuracy, 36% precision, 31% recall on one validation (a stronger judge gave 87% accuracy, 80% precision).
quote: the absence of hint words alone does not prove unfaithfulness
limits: Small to mid open models, only one thinking model (Qwen3-32B). The judge used is weak (precision 36%). The authors do not claim all chains are faithful.
agent_relevance: Hint-based G10 checks produce false alarms when the token budget is tight. If used, give a generous budget, take k samples, and add a causal check (does the answer change when the hinted fact is removed).

source: Turpin, Michael, Perez & Bowman (2023) Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
finding: Adding biasing features to few-shot prompts (answer always A; a suggested answer) changed predictions while the chain of thought never mentioned the bias.
numbers: Accuracy fell by as much as 36% on a suite of 13 tasks (BIG-Bench Hard) with GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0. 330 BBQ examples were subsampled for the stereotype tests.
quote: accuracy to drop by as much as 36%
limits: 2023 models, no reasoning models. Re-read here for abstract and headline only; the finder agents covered the detail (b27, c19).
agent_relevance: Anchor for the bias-insertion method that d03 and d05 re-test on newer models.

source: Shi, Chen, Misra, Scales, Dohan, Chi, Schaerli & Zhou (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: GSM-IC adds one irrelevant sentence to GSM8K problems. Telling the model 'Feel free to ignore irrelevant information given in the questions', adding distractor-containing exemplars, and sampling 20 answers with majority vote each helped. The instruction cost one sentence. Self-consistency cost 20 samples.
numbers: code-davinci-002, GSM-IC-4K (100 base problems). Micro accuracy: CoT 72.4 -> 77.8 with the instruction -> 88.1 with self-consistency (20 samples). LTM 77.5 -> 80.6 -> 93.4. Program prompt 54.4 -> 56.7 -> 74.6. Macro accuracy (a base problem counts only if all its variants are right): CoT 6.0 -> 15.0 (instruction) -> 30.0 (SC); LTM 18.0 -> 25.0 -> 45.0. Instruction or distractor exemplars did not lower GSM8K dev accuracy (CoT 59.3 vs 60.3). 20 samples contain the correct answer for 99.7% of problems. The generic instruction 'Solve grade school math problems.' alone did not help.
quote: Feel free to ignore irrelevant information given in the questions.
limits: 2022-era models (code-davinci-002, text-davinci-003). No 'restate the problem and strip unused quantities' step was tested; only an ignore instruction. SC cost is 20x tokens, so it is not an equal-token comparison. Complicated 4-exemplar prompts were less robust.
agent_relevance: A cheap input-hygiene sentence helps a little and sampling helps a lot, but even the best setting solves all variants for only 45% of base problems. A restate-and-strip step is still untested; test it against this instruction baseline.

source: Shi et al. (2023) GSM-IC micro vs macro accuracy (same paper, consistency measure)
finding: Per-item accuracy hides fragility. A problem counts as solved under macro accuracy only if the model is right on every irrelevant-sentence variant of that base problem. The gap between the two numbers is the single-variant versus all-variant pass gap.
numbers: Plain CoT: micro 72.4% vs macro 6.0% (code-davinci-002). Among original problems solved by greedy decoding, no more than 18% stay solved across all types of irrelevant information (key finding 1). Best macro in the table is 45% (LTM + SC).
limits: Variants are of one kind (an irrelevant sentence) from the same generator, so they are correlated. It gives no false-accept rate for a fitted rule; it gives the pass-rate gap.
agent_relevance: A held-out check on one variant lets through many answers that fail on the next. Report the all-variant pass rate, not the mean. The number of variants needed is not given anywhere in this literature.

source: Nickel, Schrewe & Flek (2024) Probing the Robustness of Theory of Mind in Large Language Models
finding: 68 hand-written ToM tasks in 10 complexity classes (transparent container, preposition replacement, late label, untrustworthy testimony, automatic state change, and so on). Per-question accuracy looks fair, but requiring every question of a scenario to be right collapses it.
numbers: Four open models (Llama 2, Vicuna-33B, Mixtral and one more). Overall turn accuracy 73.71%, 58.00%, 68.47%, 72.89%; overall goal accuracy (all scenes in a scenario right) 4.41%, 0.00%, 1.47%, 4.41%. Worst class 'automatic change knowledge': 53.75% turn accuracy for the first model.
limits: Small open models of 2023-2024, not reasoning models. 68 tasks, so goal-accuracy percentages rest on 5 to 14 scenarios per class.
agent_relevance: Second independent source for the single-variant versus all-variant gap (with d08). Use scenario-level pass as the G3 criterion.

source: Nickel, Schrewe, Mai & Flek (2026) Understanding Artificial Theory of Mind: Perturbed Tasks and Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: 1,088 hand-made false-belief items with ten perturbation classes, each annotated with the valid step-by-step belief states. Six open models, with and without chain of thought. Accuracy drops steeply under perturbation; CoT helps on average but hurts in some classes.
numbers: Models: Llama-2-70B, Vicuna-33B, Mixtral 8x7B, Yi-34B, Llama-3-70B, DBRX. Average over models, no perturbation: 67.2% plain, 89.6% with CoT. Only Llama-3-70B and DBRX meet 'limited robust ToM' (>50% on at least five of ten perturbation classes); none meets full robust ToM (>50% on all ten). By the paper's conclusion CoT helps on unperturbed items, untrustworthy testimony and unrelated information, and hurts on the control tasks, automatic change knowledge and conclusion from sentiment.
limits: No GPT, Claude, Gemini or reasoning model (the paper says so). Open-model snapshot of 2024. Class-level n is small, so most class cells have wide intervals.
agent_relevance: Best 2026 evidence that logic-preserving ToM perturbations still break models, but not for 2025 reasoning models. Do not extend it to our model; re-run on it. CoT is not a safe default scaffold for every perturbation class.

source: Kouwenhoven, van der Meer & van Duijn (2026) Traces of Social Competence in Large Language Models
finding: 17 open-weight models on 192 balanced false-belief variants. Making the mental state explicit ('X thinks') changes answers in a way scenario content does not explain. Instruction tuning partly reduces it, reasoning-oriented fine-tuning increases it. A 'think' vector steers the behaviour.
numbers: 17 open-weight models, 192 variants (Trott et al. 2023 battery); humans 83% on false belief in the original. Bayesian logistic regression: scaling helps, not strictly; the effect appears during OLMo 2 pre-training.
limits: Open-weight models only. Per-model accuracies not extracted.
agent_relevance: Reasoning fine-tuning can strengthen a surface-wording shortcut, so a wording-swap control ('thinks' vs an action verb) belongs in any ToM-style check on a reasoning model.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Reply to Hodel & West and Lewis & Mitchell. The permuted-alphabet gap, the authors argue, comes from the cost of counting positions in a shuffled alphabet. GPT-4 with code execution, used on its own without instruction, solved the counterfactual letter-string items at roughly human level.
numbers: Humans N=99 (interval 1) and N=97 (interval 2). Human vs GPT-4 main effect P=8.9e-13; human vs GPT-4+code P=0.496 (no difference). GPT-4 interval-size effect P<2e-16; with code P=0.066. 46% of GPT-4's errors (23 of 50) used a valid alternative rule, vs 39% for humans in Lewis & Mitchell.
quote: the inability of language models to solve these particular reasoning problems stems from a specific difficulty with counting
limits: By the authors of the original claim. GPT-4 with code only; no equal-token comparison; code solves counting but not the analogy rule.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a code-selected tool step shrinks a default-versus-counterfactual gap: the gap was a load problem that code removed. It does not show equal tokens, and the tool may be doing the work that matters.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using Counterfactual Tasks to Evaluate the Generality of Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Letter-string analogies with permuted or symbol alphabets. The authors added a counterfactual comprehension check (successor and predecessor questions on each letter pair of the new alphabet) to see whether the model understood the new order before blaming reasoning. Models mostly passed the check but still failed the analogies; humans did not drop.
numbers: Humans 1,876 samples, mean accuracy 0.753 [0.734, 0.773]; each GPT model 6,840 samples, mean accuracy in the range 0.35 to 0.49 (table garbled in extraction, so per-model values are not quoted). Comprehension check: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 mostly 0.9 to 1.0 on successor and predecessor. Error types: alternate rule 38.6% humans, 22% GPT-4, 5.8% GPT-3.
limits: GPT-3, 3.5, 4 of 2023. The comprehension check shows understanding of the order, not use of it with counting. Webb's reply (d12) challenges the counting step.
agent_relevance: Include a comprehension check with each counterfactual: ask for the new-order facts in isolation; if the model passes, a failure on the main item is not about misunderstanding the setup.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the Robustness of Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Extends the variant approach to digit matrices and story analogies. GPT models were sensitive to the order of the answer options and to paraphrase in story analogies, unlike humans.
numbers: GPT-4 on story analogies: 89% (16 of 18) when Story A was correct, 61% (11 of 18) when Story B was correct. Letter-string variants: humans stay high, GPT models drop sharply. Digit matrices: the drop appears on one of two variant types.
limits: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 of 2024 only. n=18 per cell for the answer-order test. No reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Answer-order swap is a cheap control for any forced-choice check in our agent: run both orders and count only answers stable under the swap.

source: Rajeev, Ramamurthy, Trivedi, Yadav et al. (2025) Cats Confuse Reasoning LLM: Query-Agnostic Adversarial Triggers for Reasoning Models (COLM 2025)
finding: Short irrelevant triggers (for example 'Interesting fact: cats sleep most of their lives') appended to maths problems raise the error rate of reasoning models. They were found with a cheap proxy model and transferred. They also lengthen the answers.
numbers: 225 problems from NuminaMath, six runs. DeepSeek R1: combined trigger error 4.50% vs 1.50% random error (3x); R1-distill-Qwen-32B 8.00% (2.83x). Cross-family on 1,000 GSM8K problems: error up to 5.14x (reasoning models) and 7.21x (Mistral-Small-24B). Slowdown (answer longer than 1.5x, 2x, 4x budget): o1 26.4%, 9.9%, 1.3%; o3-mini 16.8%, 6.0%, 3.0%; R1 28.0%, 16.2%, 4.8%; R1-distill 42.17%, 32.5%, 15.33%.
limits: The absolute increase is small (1.5% to 4.5% on R1). The attack is searched adversarially, so it overstates natural distraction. Triggers target the final answer, not a held-out rule check.
agent_relevance: A 2025 reasoning-model number for irrelevant-text sensitivity: a few points of accuracy, up to 4x tokens in a minority of cases. Token inflation matters for any equal-token comparison.

source: Yang, Huang, Zhang, Surdeanu, Wang & Pan (2025) How Is LLM Reasoning Distracted by Irrelevant Context? An Analysis Using a Controlled Benchmark (GSM-DC)
finding: Synthetic maths problems as symbolic graphs, with a set number of irrelevant nodes injected after the solution path is fixed. Accuracy falls steadily as the number of distractors rises, at fixed reasoning depth. Training with strong distractors and a process-reward-guided beam search raise out-of-distribution step accuracy.
numbers: Six models (Grok-3-Beta, GPT-4.1, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-1B). At reasoning depth 5: Grok-3-Beta step accuracy 43% with 1 irrelevant node to 19% with 15; GPT-4.1 26% to 2%. Beam search with a PRM improved OOD robustness by up to 6.29%.
limits: Synthetic symbolic graphs; no reasoning-trained models tested (R1 named as future work). Step accuracy is a strict metric.
agent_relevance: Dose-response is what an animal 'rescue version' predicts: failure scales with distractor count and length. Re-run a failed perturbed item at lower distractor count before reading it as missing rule use.

source: Dlugosz, Oliveira & Diaz-Rodriguez (2026) The Importance of Being Statistically Earnest: A Critical Re-evaluation of GSM-Symbolic
finding: Re-test of GSM-Symbolic with bootstrapped mixed models with per-question random effects. Many of the reported drops are not significant, and the new variants contain larger numbers than GSM8K, which accounts for part of the drop.
numbers: 20 open-weight models: only 8 show a significant change under the original prompt. Integer distribution shifted to larger values (Kolmogorov-Smirnov 0.12, p<0.001). Controlling for the large-number effect accounts for significance in half of the remaining cases.
limits: Open-weight models only; name/number variants, not NoOp or difficulty. Abstract and introduction read in detail, rest skimmed.
agent_relevance: A perturbation control needs its own control: check that the perturbed set matches the original on number size, length and token count, or the drop may be a difficulty effect.

source: Kutakh (2026) Reasoning, Code, or Both? How Large Language Models Handle Variations in Math Questions
finding: Claude Haiku 4.5 on 1,000 paired original and modified GSM-Symbolic problems with three scaffolds: plain CoT, PAL (single-shot code) and SBSC (iterative code). The default-versus-variant gap is already small, and code execution did not shrink it.
numbers: Original/modified accuracy: CoT 97.9/96.6 (drop 1.3 pp); PAL 97.2/95.5 (1.7); SBSC 96.4/95.0 (1.4). Items that broke: 1.8%, 3.1%, 2.5% (chi-square p=.096). Temperature 0, 8-shot.
limits: One model, grade-school problems, single run, not equal-token (code scaffolds use more calls). Differences not significant. Name/number swaps only, not distractors.
agent_relevance: On a current model the name/number gap is about 1 point, so this check cannot separate scaffolds; use harder counterfactuals (changed rules, distractors) as in d12 and d16.

source: LessWrong post (2026) Revisiting GSM-Symbolic: do 2026 frontier models still fail?
finding: The author rebuilt a GSM-NoOp set (Apple did not release one) and audited whether each added clause was really irrelevant. When only distractors judged truly irrelevant are kept, the accuracy drop for GPT-4o, Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Haiku 4.5 is near zero. Unaudited NoOp reproduces a large drop.
numbers: 1,000 questions per model (100 templates x 10); 945 distractors usable; 117 of 945 (12.4%) judged truly irrelevant by GPT-5.5; the two auditors agreed weakly (kappa=0.32; 12% vs 36% kept). Audited drops 0 to 2 points, not distinguishable from zero. Unaudited: close to the original (GPT-4o 94.9 -> 63.0 in the original paper). 8-shot CoT, last-number scoring.
limits: Blog post, not peer reviewed; only 117 audited items; per-model results are in figures I could not read; my reading is through a page-summary tool. Distractors were written by a model.
agent_relevance: Part of the NoOp drop is a labelling problem: some 'irrelevant' clauses are plausibly relevant. When building distractor controls, have a second model or a human audit that the clause truly cannot change the answer.

source: Zhang et al. (Scale AI) (2024) A Careful Examination of Large Language Model Performance on Grade School Arithmetic (GSM1k)
finding: A new benchmark of problems written from scratch to match GSM8k. Some model families (Phi, Mistral, some Llama) score lower on it than on GSM8k, which points to contamination; frontier models do not. The gap correlates with how likely a model is to generate GSM8k items.
numbers: GSM1k has 1,205 problems (the '1000' is in the name). Human distinguishability: 19 annotators found the one GSM1k item among five in 21.83% of 1,205 attempts (chance 20%). Drops up to 8%; Spearman r2=0.36 between the probability of generating GSM8k items and the GSM8k-GSM1k gap. Frontier or near-frontier models (Gemini, GPT, Claude, Mistral Large) show minimal overfitting.
limits: 2024 models. The match between sets is by human solve rates, steps and answer magnitude, not every property.
agent_relevance: Resolves the 1,000 vs 1,205 conflict: 1,205. Cheap contamination checks that transfer to our own sets: write a small fresh matched set, run a distinguishability audit, and compare likelihood of the old items.

source: Razeghi, Logan, Gardner & Singh (2022) Impact of Pretraining Term Frequencies on Few-Shot Reasoning
finding: Few-shot numerical tasks done by GPT-J and GPT-Neo models were much more accurate on instances whose numbers are common in the Pile.
numbers: Accuracy gap between the most frequent 10% and least frequent 10% of terms above 70 points (absolute) in some tasks; GPT-J-6B and GPT-Neo models trained on the Pile.
limits: The method needs the pretraining corpus to count terms, which is not available for current frontier models. I found no study that repeats it on a frontier model.
agent_relevance: Not usable as a cheap check on our own model. Substitute behavioural proxies: performance on rare vs common numbers in a fresh set (compare d17 on number size).

source: Beger, Yi, Fu, Denton, Moskvichev, Tsai, Rajamanickam & Mitchell (2026) Distinguishing Performance From Competence in Evaluations of Humanlike Abstract Reasoning (ConceptARC, NeurIPS 2026)
finding: Reasoning models (o3, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro) were tested on ConceptARC in text and image form, with and without Python and with different effort. Annotators also scored the rule each model wrote. A rule that fits the demonstrations but is not the intended concept counts as 'correct-unintended'. In text, a large share of correct outputs rest on such rules. In image form, accuracy falls but the stated rules are often right.
numbers: o3 text pass@1: 77.1% medium effort, 68.3% low; with Python 75.6% and 67.9%. About 27% of o3's correct text outputs (and Gemini's) rest on correct-unintended or incorrect rules; Claude about 19%; humans about 7% (but 19% of human rules were unclear). Visual: o3 29.2% output accuracy but 40.0% correct-intended rules (difference 10.8 points); Claude 6.9% vs 14.4%; Gemini 5.8% vs 23.5%. Rule annotation agreement 84.8%, kappa 0.70. 480 ConceptARC tasks.
quote: using performance (accuracy) alone can substantially overestimate AI competence in textual modalities
limits: Manual rule coding on a subset; human rule data only for correct outputs. Does not compare surface re-coding, mutated inputs and symmetry checks head to head, so gap 5 is not closed.
agent_relevance: The best measured false-pass rate for ARC-style tasks: about one in four correct answers is a shortcut. A rule-level audit (ask for the rule, then judge it against the intended concept or a held-out variant) is a control we can run; colour-permutation or mutation controls remain untested head to head.

source: Bastos, Wood & Taylor (2021) Kea (Nestor notabilis) fail a loose-string connectivity task
finding: Kea failed a horizontal task where only one of two loose strings was attached, both before and after a phase of perceptual-motor feedback experience. The authors say feedback alone cannot explain the pattern.
numbers: Not in the page text (abstract only).
limits: Taylor group (same as K08). Abstract page only; kea sample size not seen.
agent_relevance: Even inside the Taylor group the feedback-loop account is not a full explanation. Do not model a single deterministic alternative explanation.

source: Smirnova, Cheplakova & Kubenko (2025) Some Hooded crows (Corvus cornix) understand how a loose string works (Sci Rep)
finding: Independent lab (Lomonosov Moscow State University). Six hooded crows got three loose-string tasks meant to test whether they grasp the causal basis rather than a learned rule. None solved either of the first two spontaneously, individual learning took hundreds of trials, and in the critical Phase 3 (an extra, unconnected short string) the authors say only that some crows 'may have begun to understand'.
numbers: Six crows. Phase 1 (30 different stoppers): none chose the correct end above chance in session 1; training criterion 9 of 10 consecutive trials (p=0.022). Phase 2 standard loose string: 105 to 243 trials to learn to pull both ends (rooks and parrots similar; chimpanzees 5 to 10 trials). Phase 3: 2 sessions x 30 trials, chance 33% or 66% by condition, binomial tests per bird.
quote: some crows may have begun to understand how the loose string works
limits: Loose-string (cooperation) task, not the classic vertical or horizontal task of Taylor and Heinrich. N=6 and within-bird tests only. The authors state that associative learning from perceptual-motor feedback is hard to separate from understanding.
agent_relevance: Independent-lab evidence points the same way as Taylor's: slow learning, strong individual differences, partial transfer. It does not resolve insight versus feedback; plan controls that assume both can coexist.

source: Baciadonna, Cornero, Clayton & Emery (2022) Mirror-mediated string-pulling task in Eurasian jays (Garrulus glandarius)
finding: A horizontal string-pulling task where the food could be seen only in a mirror. Four jays learned to pull the right string with direct view; none used the reflection. The authors cannot say whether the birds lacked the concept or the setup removed the visual-perceptual-motor feedback.
numbers: Four birds learned the direct-view version; zero used the mirror-reflected information.
limits: Cambridge lab (not Taylor). Abstract only read for outcome. Mirror use is a different ability from string-pulling insight.
agent_relevance: A second independent group states that removing feedback and removing understanding cannot be told apart in one setup: a control must vary the feedback while keeping the structure fixed.
